840688.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following release from State requisition
840688.issue: Why did protection against wrongful dispossession not establish the former lessees entitlement to receive possession after requisition ended?
840688.subject: Mimanis
840688.property: Mangla Hat, No. 1 Strand Road, Howrah
records: The judgment records a fifty-year lease beginning on 1 January 1939, with no renewal clause, expiring on 31 December 1988.
The State took possession under requisition on 25 November 1987 while the lease was still in force.
The first High Court order directed restoration to the owner or occupier as appropriate; the later order directed delivery to owners while reserving further remedies.
Counsel for the Mimanis argued that possession should return to the person from whom it was taken and that the first judgment could not be reopened by liberty to mention.
The Supreme Court regarded reopening through liberty to apply as unwarranted, but addressed the merits itself under Article 136 after extensive argument and elapsed time.
The Court distinguished a lessee remaining in possession after expiry from the Mimanis, who were already out of possession under requisition.
The Court treated entitlement at restoration as requiring examination rather than automatic return to the person dispossessed by requisition.
The Court preserved the parties ability to pursue appropriate proceedings and any agreement for purchase; that reservation did not itself establish entitlement to possession.
rules: Juridical protection from wrongful dispossession does not by itself establish lawful entitlement to receive property after requisition and expiry of a lease.
Target factual conjunction: State possession, expired lease without renewal, restoration stage. Do not generalize to forcible eviction of an occupant.
Liberty to mention cannot reopen a decided matter; the Court nevertheless considered the merits under Article 136 in this procedural setting.
The procedural criticism and merits disposition coexist; neither deletes the other.
gaps: The rendered text has apparent OCR inconsistencies in statutory subsection references and years (including L84, L172 and L187). Preserve them; do not approve a corrected statutory formula without an authoritative check.
Original lease, correspondence and requisition order were not independently obtained.
OPEN_TEXT assessment required; no general automatic rule equating lease expiry with lawful forcible eviction.
840688.boundary: Reconstruct refusal of automatic restoration in this requisition setting, not a universal denial of possessory protection.

161859415.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal from revision in a Section 6 summary suit
161859415.issue: How can a landlord seek recovery when a third party forcibly dispossesses the tenant, and why is tenant joinder not invariably necessary?
161859415.subject: Anita Anant Sawant
161859415.property: Suit rooms in House No. 97, Ambet
records: The plaintiff alleged purchase of House No. 97, later letting of the suit rooms to P.V. Warik, and his forcible dispossession by the defendants on 1 October 1988.
The contesting defendants claimed joint-family ownership and possession; the vendor challenged consideration and alleged fraud.
The trial court found dispossession proved and treated the landlady as possessing through her tenant.
The High Court rejected the argument that only the physically dispossessed tenant could sue.
The judgment records earlier Madras and Nagpur views denying or restricting the landlord remedy; these are opposing authorities, not facts of this dispute.
Earlier courts as reported by target
The target Court held that letting changes the mode of possession and that third-party dispossession of the tenant is also dispossession of the landlord for this remedy.
The Court distinguished desirable joinder from an absolute necessity; tenant non-joinder is not fatal to maintainability in the stated setting.
Section 6 as reproduced preserves a separate title suit; the trial title issue was described as unnecessary.
rules: A landlord retaining legal possession through a tenant may maintain Section 6 recovery against a third party who forcibly dispossessed that tenant.
Maintainability only. Section 6 time limit, consent, due-course-of-law and government exclusion remain; title is not adjudicated by this rule.
Tenant joinder may be desirable but is not an absolute prerequisite for the stated landlord Section 6 suit.
Do not translate not necessary into always irrelevant; retain the concrete third-party dispossession setting.
gaps: The target states the dispossession date but does not supply the filing date in the selected account; do not independently certify six-month compliance merely from the result.
Earlier cited decisions and original exhibits have not been separately verified.
161859415.boundary: Maintainability through legal possession and non-fatal nonjoinder; not proof of ownership or a new general ejectment entitlement.

74028.stage: Supreme Court appeal concerning interlocutory mandatory injunction, merits reserved
74028.issue: Why did the Court reject the High Court interim restoration order without finally deciding contractual revocation or possession at trial?
74028.subject: Sriman Narayan
74028.opponent: Hindustan Petroleum Corporation and AP State Civil Supplies Corporation
records: The suit sought interim protection of the petrol pump possession and business; the challenged orders included restoration.
The plaintiff asserted continuing possession until forcible dispossession on 29 September 2000 after suit was filed.
The defendant asserted takeover on 22 September 2000 and delivery to the second defendant.
The trial court relied on the listed documents and accepted the 22 September takeover account, finding no strong prima facie case.
The High Court regarded termination as prima facie illegal and the plaintiff as in possession when suit was filed, granting interim relief.
Andhra Pradesh High Court as reported
The target Court recorded the conceded change from proprietary firm to partnership and the contractual revocation clause; its view of entitlement to act was expressly prima facie.
The Court criticized failure to address contrary trial reasons and whether damages would adequately compensate refusal of interim relief.
The Court reserved contract validity for trial and expressly stated its observations would not affect the merits.
rules: Interim injunction requires prima facie case, balance of convenience and irreparable injury assessed pending unresolved rights.
Discretionary interlocutory test, not deterministic merits adjudication.
Mandatory interim relief generally requires a strong case, serious non-compensable injury and balance of convenience, subject to judicial discretion and exceptional circumstances.
Dorab is reported in this judgment, not independently obtained here. Preserve non-exhaustive and non-absolute character.
gaps: Conflicting possession accounts remain trial questions, not facts resolved for all purposes by this interlocutory disposition.
Underlying agreement and exhibits B-3 through B-9 not independently obtained.
No numeric weighting or automatic conjunction can substitute for equitable discretion.
74028.boundary: Interim relief only; neither a final contractual validity ruling nor final ownership/possession adjudication.

522414.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal concerning recovery of possession after claimed forcible dispossession
522414.issue: Why did the discrepancy between plot numbers 160 and 1060 not defeat recovery of plot 1060?
522414.subject: Santchara Kuer respondents
records: The respondents sought declaration, ejectment and mesne profits after their account of auction purchase, onward sale and forcible dispossession.
The Court confined discussion to three disputed plots, while the selected reconstruction concerns plot 1060 only.
The appellants argued that plot 1060 appeared in neither the sale decree nor certificate, both listing 160.
The High Court found matching khata number, area and boundaries for plot 1060 despite the numeric discrepancy.
The target Court emphasized that no plot 160 existed in khata 97 and treated the missing zero as misdescription.
The High Court account also identifies the correct plot in delivery writ and onward sale deed.
The Court distinguished reconstructing sale scope by going behind the certificate from resolving the present misdescription on the stated identifying particulars.
The Court cautioned that the matter might differ if boundaries were absent and only the plot number appeared.
rules: A misdescription may be treated as irregularity where identity is not doubtful; a change in the identity of property sold is different.
Restricted to identification from the actual decree/certificate particulars; never merge objects by similar names alone.
The plot 1060 conclusion rests on matching area, khata and boundaries plus absence of a rival plot 160 in that khata.
Case-specific judicial assessment reconstruction; not a universal cadastral matching algorithm. Other plots have separate mortgage issues.
gaps: Original decree, sale certificate, delivery writ and cadastral records were not independently obtained.
Other plots 427 and 1128 are not part of this selected chain and cannot inherit its result.
Judicially accepted identity must not be represented as program verification of the original instruments.
522414.boundary: Identity objection concerning plot 1060 only; no automatic resolution of every plot or title dispute.

1144022.stage: Supreme Court two conflicting opinions and larger-bench referral
1144022.issue: How do the two opinions differ about dispossession, licence expiry and Section 6 protection, and why can neither be presented as the Bench unified merits holding?
1144022.subject: Syndicate Bank
records: Kasliwal J records the licence period and refused renewal; the bank continued occupation after expiry.
The first opinion records fire, continued presence of records and furniture, restricted access, and later refusal of entry.
The proceeding was tried on counsel willingness, without prejudice, to proceed on dispossession as alleged; the opinions differ in the legal treatment of that concession.
The High Court treated the bank as in settled possession and granted the Section 6 remedy.
Kasliwal J regarded the bank as having vacated due to fire and denied Section 6 relief in these circumstances despite acknowledged ownership and licence expiry.
Kasliwal J separate opinion, not Bench holding
Ramaswamy J relied on the procedural concession, retained intention to possess and absence of due process, reaching the opposite view of Section 6 protection.
Ramaswamy J separate opinion, not Bench holding
The company argued voluntary vacating and no juridical possession; the bank relied on the concession and settled possession.
The second opinion distinguished the summary possession route from title litigation and treated lease/licence classification in the regular suit as unresolved there.
rules: Kasliwal J would refuse Section 6 relief on his assessment of licence expiry, fire-related vacating and absence of force or unlawful dispossession.
Opinion-specific proposed rule; NOT a unified holding or approved precedent. No conclusion from the companion opinion may be spliced into this chain.
Ramaswamy J would protect settled possession against dispossession without consent otherwise than due process, applying the concession and preserved intention to possess.
Opinion-specific proposed rule; NOT a unified holding. Preserve six-month and government exclusions and distinction from title proceedings.
gaps: The available document ends in a larger-bench referral, not a unified merits decision; no follow-up is obtained in this batch.
Rendered dates and phrases differ between opinions (including expiry and without/with prejudice wording). Retain exact text and flag for authoritative source checking.
Neither original licence nor letters nor trial transcript independently obtained.
1144022.boundary: Reconstruct both opinion-specific chains and the unresolved Bench conflict; do not manufacture a final winner.
